sources: Office of the Historian, US Department of State, 'The Gulf of Tonkin Incident, 1964': the destroyers Maddox and Turner Joy reported attacks by North Vietnamese patrol boats on August 2 and a second on August 4, 1964; historians later questioned whether the second attack took place; Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution on August 7, the House unanimously and the Senate with only two votes against; it let the president take any measures he deemed necessary and preceded Rolling Thunder and ground troop deployments; https://history.state.gov/milestones/1961-1968/gulf-of-tonkin

National Security Archive (George Washington University), 'Tonkin Gulf Intelligence Skewed According to Official History and Intercepts' (Dec 1, 2005): NSA declassified Robert Hanyok's history; SIGINT shows a second attack on August 4, 1964 'did not occur'; torpedo boats did attack the Maddox on August 2; 'the overwhelming body of reports, if used, would have told the story that no attack occurred'; NSA deputy director Louis Tordella was quoted in 1972 saying the 4 August intercepts pertained to the 2 August attacks; https://nsarchive2.gwu.edu/NSAEBB/NSAEBB132/press20051201.htm

Council on Foreign Relations, 'TWE Remembers: The Gulf of Tonkin Incident': Maddox reported unidentified ships at 8:40 p.m. Aug 4 and maneuvered for about three hours against perceived attacks; Capt. Herrick's message: 'Freak weather effects on radar and overeager sonarmen may have accounted for many reports' and 'No actual visual sightings by MADDOX'; pilot overhead James Stockdale saw 'no boats, no boat wakes, no boat gunfire, no torpedo wakes, nothing but black sea and American firepower'; at 11:30 p.m. Johnson went on national TV announcing air strikes; Johnson later: 'those damn, stupid sailors were just shooting at flying fish'; https://www.cfr.org/articles/twe-remembers-gulf-tonkin-incident

beats.say: What if I told you America went to war over a sea battle that never happened?
August 1964. The destroyer Maddox is on a spy patrol off North Vietnam.
On August second, three torpedo boats really do attack it. The Maddox drives them off.
Two nights later, it is back with a second destroyer. A pitch-black, stormy night.
Then the radar lights up. Boats! Torpedoes!
For hours, both ships fire at targets nobody can see.
Then the captain warns, freak weather and overeager sonarmen may explain the reports. Nobody saw a boat.
A pilot flying overhead saw no boats. No wakes. Nothing but black sea.
Too late. That night, the President went on TV and announced air strikes.
Three days later, Congress gave him power to fight. Not one House member voted no.
That vote opened the door to the Vietnam War.
In 2005, the NSA released its own secret history.
Its verdict? The second attack never happened.
The intercepts that seemed to prove it were about the first fight.
Would you have trusted the radar?
Even the President later grumbled, they were just shooting at flying fish.
